Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 59:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days; then He established Himself on the Throne, the Most Merciful, so ask about Him one who is informed﴾ (25:59).

Says He, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And put your trust in the Living One who does not die﴾ ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾, then said: ﴿and what is between them﴾, though the heavens and the earth had been mentioned. The heavens are a plural collective, and He directed the pronoun to the two kinds and the two things, as al-Qutami said:

"Did it not grieve you that the ropes of Qays ... and Taghlib have become severed, separated in severance?" [[The line is by al-Qutami, and its discussion has been given in detail earlier. The point of evidence here: the poet said "tabayannata" (in the dual) although "hibal" (ropes) is a plural of "habl" (rope). The justification for this is that the ropes of Qays are one group and the ropes of Taghlib are another group, so he treated them, in the return of the pronoun to them, as two singular things. Its like in the Qur'an: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, because He directed that to the two qualities.]]

He means: "and the ropes of Taghlib," so he used the dual, and "hibal" is a plural, because he intended the two things and the two kinds.

* *

As for His words: ﴿in six days﴾

It has been said: the beginning of that was on Sunday, and the completion on Friday. ﴿Then He established Himself on the Throne, the Most Merciful﴾ means: then He established Himself on the Throne, the Most Merciful, and rose above it, and that was on Saturday, it is said.

* *

As for His words: ﴿so ask about Him one who is informed﴾

It means: so ask, O Muhammad, one informed about the Most Merciful, informed about His creation, for He is the Creator of everything, and nothing He has created is hidden from Him.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the exegetes) said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words: ﴿so ask about Him one who is informed﴾: He said: he says to Muhammad ﷺ: when I inform you of something, know that it is as I have informed you. I am the Informed (al-Khabir). And "khabiran" in His words ﴿so ask about Him one who is informed﴾ is in the accusative as a state (hal) of the pronoun "hu" in His words "bihi" (about Him).

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion﴾ (25:60).

Says He, may His remembrance be exalted: And when it is said to these who worship besides Allah what does not benefit them nor harm them: ﴿Prostrate to the Most Merciful﴾, meaning: make your prostration sincerely for Allah, apart from the gods and idols. They say: ﴿Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of Madinah and Basra read ﴿limā ta'murunā﴾ ("what you command us") meaning: shall we prostrate, O Muhammad, to what you command us to prostrate to. The majority of the reciters of Kufa read "limā ya'murunā" with the yā' (what the Most Merciful commands), and some of them mentioned that Musaylimah was called "the Most Merciful," so when the Prophet ﷺ said to them "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they said: "Shall we prostrate to what the Most Merciful of Yamamah commands us?" meaning Musaylimah by prostrating to him.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: the correct view regarding this is that both are widely transmitted, well-known readings, and scholars among the reciters have read each of them, so whichever one the reader recites is correct.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And it increases them in aversion﴾

It means: the saying of the one who says to these polytheists, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," increased them, by sincere prostration to Allah and singling Allah out for worship, in distance from what they were called to, in flight.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 25, verses 60–61:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Blessed is He who has placed in the sky great stars (buruj), and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: The Lord is holy, who has placed in the sky buruj. By buruj, some say, is meant palaces.

Mention of those who said this:

• Muhammad ibn al-'Ala', Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Salm ibn Janada narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard my father, from 'Atiyyah ibn Sa'd, concerning His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who has placed in the sky buruj﴾, he said: Palaces in the sky, in which are the guards.

• Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to me, saying: Isma'il narrated to me, from Yahya ibn Rafi', concerning His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who has placed in the sky buruj﴾, he said: Palaces in the sky.

• Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Amr, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿placed in the sky buruj﴾, he said: Palaces in the sky.

• Isma'il ibn Sayf narrated to me, saying: 'Ali ibn Mushir narrated to me, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, concerning His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who has placed in the sky buruj﴾, he said: Palaces in the sky, in which are the guards.

Others said: They are the great stars.

Mention of those who said this:

• Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ya'la ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: Isma'il narrated to us, from Abu Salih: ﴿Blessed is He who has placed in the sky buruj﴾, he said: The great stars.

• He said: al-Dahhak narrated to us, from Makhlad, from 'Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, he said: The planets.

• al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿buruj﴾, he said: The buruj are the stars.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The more correct of the two opinions in this matter is the view of those who said: They are palaces in the sky, because this is the usage of the Arabs, as in ﴿And even if you were in towers built high﴾, and the saying of al-Akhtal:

"As if it were a Roman tower that a builder erected with plaster, bricks and stones."

[The line is by al-Akhtal, as the author stated. Al-burj is here meant as a palace, as he said. It is frequent in Arabic usage to liken strong, well-tied travelling camels to Roman buildings, and among this is the saying of Tarafah describing his she-camel: "Like the arch of the Roman, whose owner swore that it would be completed, until it is built with tile."

The line is evidence that burj means palace.]

By burj is meant a palace.

* *

His saying: ﴿and placed therein a lamp﴾

The reciters differed regarding the reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra read ﴿sirajan﴾ in the singular, and they interpreted it as meaning that He placed therein the sun, which is the lamp meant by His saying: ﴿and placed therein a lamp﴾.

As such:

• al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾, he said: The lamp is the sun.

The majority of the reciters of Kufa read "wa-ja'ala fiha sururjan" [sujuran], in the plural, as though they interpreted it to mean: and placed therein stars, ﴿and a luminous moon﴾, and they took the stars to be lamps, since one is guided by them.

The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is to say: these are two well-known readings among the readings of the regions, and each has an understandable meaning; whichever of the two a reciter reads, he is correct.

* *

His saying: ﴿and a luminous moon﴾

By al-munir is meant the shining.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day to succeed each other, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾ (25:62).

The scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of His words: ﴿made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is that God made each of them a successor (khalf) to the other, in that whatever deed one of them caused a person to miss, which could be done for God, could be made up in the other.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Hafs ibn Humayd, from Shamir ibn 'Atiyyah, from Shaqiq, who said: A man came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "I missed the prayer last night." He said: "Make up what you missed of your night during your day, for Allah made the night and the day a succession (khilfah) for whoever wishes to remember, or wishes to be grateful."

'Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾, he said: whoever misses something of the night may do it during the day, or of the day he may make it up during the night.

al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan, regarding His words: ﴿made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾, he said: He made one of them a successor to the other: if a man misses something during the day, he makes it up at night, and if he misses something at night, he makes it up during the day.

Others said: rather, its meaning is that He made each of them differ from its companion, so this one is black and this one is white.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿the night and the day succeeding one another﴾, he said: black and white.

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the same.

Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Umar ibn Qays ibn Abi Muslim al-Masir, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾, he said: black and white.

Others said: rather, the meaning is that each of them succeeds the other: when this goes, that comes, and when that comes, this goes.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Qays narrated to us, from 'Umar ibn Qays al-Masir, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾, he said: this succeeds that, and that succeeds this.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day succeeding one another﴾: "Had He not made them succeed one another, one would not know how to act. If the age were all night, how would anyone know how to fast; or if the age were all day, how would anyone know how to pray." He said: "Khalfah means: two alternating things, one goes and the other comes; God made them a succession for the servants." And he recited: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾. The word khilfah is a verbal noun (masdar), which is why it is singular, and it is a predicate about the night and the day. The Arabs say: "Khalafa hadha min kadha khilfah," meaning when one thing comes in place of another that went before it, as the poet said:

"For her, at al-Matirun, when the ants have eaten what they had gathered, is a khilfah (alternation), until, when she has entered spring, she settles from Jilaq in the churches (bay')."

[[The two verses are attributed to Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah from a poem of his that the author of Khizanat al-Adab al-Kubra (3: 278–280) mentioned, composed in amorous verse about a Christian woman who had taken up monastic life in a monastery at al-Matirun, a garden on the outskirts of Damascus. In the verses "kharfah" appears in place of "khilfah," and kharafah with a dammed kha': what is plucked and gathered; this is the transmission of al-Mubarrad in al-Kamil. The author's transmission agrees with that of the author of al-Ubab, and al-Ayni also narrated it thus from Abu al-Qawtiyah, saying: the reading is "al-khilfah" with lam, which is what comes forth of fruit after the good fruit. al-Baghdadi said: the sound reading in my view is "khilfah," as a noun of ikhtilaf, meaning alternation. "Irtaba'at" means she entered the spring season. It is also reported as "rabi'at," with the same meaning. It is also reported as "dhakarat" in place of "sakanat." "Jilaq" is a city in Syria, and "al-bay'" is the plural of bay'ah (with kasra on the ba'), a place of worship. al-Jawhari, and the authors of al-Ubab and al-Misbah, said: it is for the Christians; al-Ayni said: the bay'ah is for the Jews, and the church is for the Christians, but this does not fit his statement that the poem is about a Christian woman. The meaning of the two verses is that this woman frequents al-Matirun in winter, when the ants store grain in summer to eat in winter; and when she enters the days of spring, she travels to the churches in Jilaq. End. The author cited the poem as evidence for the meaning of khilfah as explained by al-Baghdadi.]] And as Zuhayr said:

"Among them the wild cows and the gazelles walk in succession, and their young rise from every resting place."

[[The verse is from the mu'allaqah of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma (Mukhtar Shi'r al-Jahili, with the commentary of Mustafa al-Saqqa, published by Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi and sons, p. 228). Its commentator said: "al-'ayn" is the plural of 'ayna', wild cows. "al-aram" is the plural of ram, a gazelle of pure white. "Khilfah": some succeed others. "al-atla'" is the plural of tala', the young of cloven-hoofed animals. "al-majthim" is the resting place. The evidence in the verse, according to the author, is in his words "khilfah," as in the previous evidence: that is, some go and others succeed them."]]

By His words "walking in succession" he means: a group goes away from them, and another group comes to replace it. It is also possible that Zuhayr meant by "khilfah": of differing colors, varieties in their colors and forms. And it is possible that he meant that they go in their walking thus, and come thus.

* *

As for His words: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾:

He, may He be exalted, says: He made the night and the day, and the succession of each of them after the other, a proof and a sign for whoever wishes to remember the command of Allah, so that he turns in repentance to the truth; ﴿or wishes to be grateful﴾, or wishes to thank Allah for the blessing He bestowed upon him in the alternation of night and day.

The scholars of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿or wishes to be grateful﴾, he said: to thank his Lord for His blessing upon him in both.

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾, that is a sign for him, ﴿or wishes to be grateful﴾, he said: to thank his Lord for His blessing upon him in both.

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of His words: ﴿yadhdhakkara﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Basra, and some of the Kufans, read it with shaddah (yadhdhakkara), meaning "yatadhakkara" (takes heed). The majority of the Kufan reciters read "yadhkura" without shaddah. The shaddah and its absence may have the same meaning in such a case; it is said: "dhakartu hajat fulan" and "tadhakkartuha," meaning I remembered the need of so-and-so.

The position on this is that they are two well-known recitations, close in meaning, and whichever of them the reciter reads, he is correct in both.

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾

Says the Exalted: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, with forbearance, tranquility and dignity, not arrogant, not tyrannical, and not striving in it through corruption and disobedience to God.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) said similarly to what we have said, but they differed. Some of them said: By His words ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾ He means that they walk upon it with tranquility and dignity.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: with dignity and tranquility.

He said: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Abd al-Karim, from Mujahid: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: with forbearance and dignity.

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: with dignity and tranquility.

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from al-Thawri, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿walk upon it in humility﴾, with dignity and tranquility.

Yahya ibn Talha al-Yarbu'i related to me, saying: Sharik related to us, from Salim, from Sa'id and Abd al-Rahman: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, they both said: with tranquility and dignity.

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Sharik, from Jabir, from Ammar, from Ikrima, regarding His words: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: with dignity and tranquility.

He said: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Hakkam related to us, from Ayyub, from Amr al-Mala'i: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: with dignity and tranquility.

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is that they walk upon it in obedience and humility.

Mention of those who said this:

Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾: with obedience, chastity and humility.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: they walk upon the earth in obedience.

Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman related to me, saying: my paternal uncle Abdullah ibn Wahb related to me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Suwayd wrote to me, saying: I heard Zayd ibn Aslam say: I sought the interpretation of this verse, ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, but I did not find it with anyone. Then I was shown in a dream and it was said to me: They are those who do not desire to corrupt the earth.

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Usama ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, he said: They do not corrupt the earth.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: They do not behave arrogantly towards people, nor are they tyrannical, nor do they corrupt. And he recited the saying of God: ﴿That is the abode of the Hereafter; We assign it to those who do not desire haughtiness upon the earth or corruption, and the ultimate outcome is for the righteous.﴾

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is that they walk upon it with forbearance, not acting ignorantly towards one who acts ignorantly towards them.

Mention of those who said this:

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Yaman related to us, from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan, regarding ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: They are forbearing; if ignorance is directed at them, they do not act ignorantly.

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, from Yazid, from Ikrima, ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: forbearing.

al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan, regarding His words: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾, he said: learned and forbearing, they do not act ignorantly.

And His words: ﴿and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾

He says: And when the ignorant, those ignorant of God, address them with what they dislike of speech, they respond to them with what is good in speech and sound address.

The people of ta'wil said similarly to what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak related to us, from Ma'mar, from Yahya ibn al-Mukhtar, from al-Hasan, regarding His words: ﴿and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾, he said: The believers are a people who are docile. Whoever does not console himself with the consolation of God will have his soul consumed by regret over the world, and whoever sees no blessing of God upon him except in food and drink, his knowledge has diminished and his punishment is near.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾, he said: sound speech.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Abd al-Karim, from Mujahid, ﴿and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾, he said: sound speech.

al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from al-Thawri, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, ﴿and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾, forbearing.

He said: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman related to us, from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan, who said: They are forbearing and do not act ignorantly; if ignorance is directed at them, they bear it patiently and do not act foolishly. This is their daytime, so how is their night, the best night? They set their feet in prayer and let their tears flow down their cheeks, seeking from God, exalted is His praise, the freeing of their necks.

He said: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Abbad informed us, from al-Hasan, who said: They are forbearing and do not act ignorantly, and if ignorance is directed at them, they bear it patiently.

The interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing (in prayer) (64). And those who say: "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-clinging (ghuram) (65). Indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode (66)﴾.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And those who spend the night before their Lord" means they pray to God, alternating between prostration in their prayer and standing.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and standing﴾: it is the plural of *qa'im* (one standing), just as *siyam* is the plural of *sa'im* (one fasting). ﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell"﴾ means: those who ask God to turn away from them His retribution and punishment, out of fear of it and dread.

* *

As for His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging (kana gharaman)﴾:

He means: the punishment of Hell is *gharaman*, a constant, persistent, inescapable clinging that never leaves those among the disbelievers who are punished by it, and destroys them. From the same root comes the saying "a man is *mughram*," meaning one burdened with debt (*al-ghurm* and *al-dayn*). From it is also called the creditor a *gharim*, because of his demand for his right and his insistence upon it from his debtor. From it is also said of a man who is infatuated with women: "He is *mughram* with women," and "so-and-so is *mughram* with so-and-so" when he cannot bear to be without him. From it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"If he punishes, his punishment will be *gharaman*, and if he gives generously, he will not care."

He means: if he punishes, his punishment will be a binding punishment that does not leave its object, destroying him.

And the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"And on the day of al-Nissar and the day of al-Jifar, there was punishment, and there was *gharam*."

[The verse is by Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, as the author says. In *al-Lisan* it is attributed to al-Tirimmah. It says: *al-gharam* is the binding punishment, lasting evil, affliction, love, passion, and what cannot be escaped. Al-Zajjaj said it is the most severe punishment in the language. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾. He also said: "And the day of al-Nissar..." And His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾ mean: constant, persistent, and binding. In al-Bakri's *Mu'jam maAsta'jam* (Cairo edition, p. 385), *al-Jifar* with a kasra on its first letter and the letter *ra* is a place in Najd, and it is the place Bishr ibn Abi Khazim meant in his words: "And the day of al-Jifar..." Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Jifar is in the lands of Banu Tamim. Al-Bakri said in the entry on al-Nissar: al-Nissar, with a kasra on its first letter, in the form of a plural, are small mountains likened to a vulture that has alighted. Abu Hatim mentioned this. He said elsewhere: they are three black rocky hills called *al-Ansur*. There Tayy, Asad and Ghatafan, who were allies of Banu 'Amir and Banu Tamim, attacked, and Tamim fled while Banu 'Amir held firm, and they killed them severely. Banu Tamim were angered on behalf of Banu 'Amir, gathered, and met them at the day of al-Jifar, where they suffered worse than Banu 'Amir had. Bishr ibn Abi Khazim said: "Tamim was angered that 'Amir was slain on the day of al-Nissar, so they were recompensed with al-Sayhalam."

I say: *al-Sayhalam* is the destroying calamity. In another narration: "fa-u'tibu" (they were given recompense).]

And it is said in the same sense: the punishment of Hell is ever-clinging for those who are in it.

With the like of what we have said concerning this, the people of *ta'wil* (interpretation) have said.

Mention of those who said so:

* Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Lani narrated to me, saying: al-Mu'afi ibn Imran al-Mawsili informed us, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: God questioned the disbelievers about His blessings, and they did not return them to Him, so He made them debtors (*aghramahum*), and He caused them to enter the Fire.

* He said: al-Mu'afi narrated to us from Abu al-Ash'hab, from al-Hasan, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: They knew that every creditor parts from his debtor, except the creditor of Hell.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾: *al-gharam* is evil.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: it does not part from him.

* *

As for His words, ﴿indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode﴾:

He says: indeed Hell is evil as a *mustaqarr* (place of settling) and *muqam* (place of abode). By *mustaqarr* He means the settled place (*al-qarar*), and by *muqam* the dwelling (*al-iqamah*). The meaning of the speech is as if to say: Hell is evil as a dwelling and a resting place. If the *mim* of *muqam* is vowelled with a *damma*, it is from *iqamah*; if it is vowelled with a *fatha*, it is from *qumtu* (I stood). It is also said that *muqam* with a *fatha* on the *mim* means a sitting place (*majlis*). From *muqam* with a *damma* in the sense of *iqamah*, is the verse of Salamah ibn Jandal:

"Two days: a day of gatherings and assemblies, and a day of marching against the enemies, returning at dusk."

[The verse is by Salamah ibn Jandal, as the author said. (See *al-Lisan*, root *a-w-b*.) *Al-muqamat* is the plural of *muqamah*, meaning *iqamah*. *Ta'wib* in the language of the Arabs means marching the whole day until night. He says: we pass our lives in this way: we make one day for dwelling, when the men of judgment among us gather in their assemblies to consult and to arrange the affairs of the tribe; and the other day we make for raiding the enemies, attacking them, and even if we march to them the whole day, we do not care, for we are people of might and protection. The author cited it at His words, describing Hell: ﴿indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode﴾, meaning a dwelling.]

And from *muqam* in the sense of a sitting place is the verse of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"Whichever of us, you or I, was the worse, let him be led to the *maqamah* (assembly), not seeing it."

[The verse is by 'Abbas ibn Mirdas, which Ibn Barri cited in *al-Lisan* (root *q-w-m*), and it is evidence that *al-maqam* and *al-maqamah*, with a *fatha* on the *mim*, mean a sitting place. Al-Baghdadi said in *al-Khizanah* (2:230): he invokes curse upon whichever of them is the worse, meaning: whoever among us is worse, may God blind him in this world, so that he does not see until he is led to his assembly. The commentator on *al-Lubab* said: that is, he is led to the places where people stand and gather on the plains, not seeing them, i.e., a blind man who cannot see the assembly. The verse is one of several by 'Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami, which he composed for Khafaf ibn Nadbah concerning a dispute between them.]

He means: the assembly.

* He said: al-Mu'afi narrated to us from Abu al-Ash'hab, from al-Hasan, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: They knew that every creditor parts from his debtor, except the creditor of Hell.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾: *al-gharam* is evil.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: it does not part from him.

* *

As for His words, ﴿indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode﴾:

He says: indeed Hell is evil as a *mustaqarr* (place of settling) and *muqam* (place of abode). By *mustaqarr* He means the settled place (*al-qarar*), and by *muqam* the dwelling (*al-iqamah*). The meaning of the speech is as if to say: Hell is evil as a dwelling and a resting place. If the *mim* of *muqam* is vowelled with a *damma*, it is from *iqamah*; if it is vowelled with a *fatha*, it is from *qumtu* (I stood). It is also said that *muqam* with a *fatha* on the *mim* means a sitting place (*majlis*). From *muqam* with a *damma* in the sense of *iqamah*, is the verse of Salamah ibn Jandal:

"Two days: a day of gatherings and assemblies, and a day of marching against the enemies, returning at dusk."

[The verse is by Salamah ibn Jandal, as the author said. (See *al-Lisan*, root *a-w-b*.) *Al-muqamat* is the plural of *muqamah*, meaning *iqamah*. *Ta'wib* in the language of the Arabs means marching the whole day until night. He says: we pass our lives in this way: we make one day for dwelling, when the men of judgment among us gather in their assemblies to consult and to arrange the affairs of the tribe; and the other day we make for raiding the enemies, attacking them, and even if we march to them the whole day, we do not care, for we are people of might and protection. The author cited it at His words, describing Hell: ﴿indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode﴾, meaning a dwelling.]

And from *muqam* in the sense of a sitting place is the verse of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"Whichever of us, you or I, was the worse, let him be led to the *maqamah* (assembly), not seeing it."

[The verse is by 'Abbas ibn Mirdas, which Ibn Barri cited in *al-Lisan* (root *q-w-m*), and it is evidence that *al-maqam* and *al-maqamah*, with a *fatha* on the *mim*, mean a sitting place. Al-Baghdadi said in *al-Khizanah* (2:230): he invokes curse upon whichever of them is the worse, meaning: whoever among us is worse, may God blind him in this world, so that he does not see until he is led to his assembly. The commentator on *al-Lubab* said: that is, he is led to the places where people stand and gather on the plains, not seeing them, i.e., a blind man who cannot see the assembly. The verse is one of several by 'Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami, which he composed for Khafaf ibn Nadbah concerning a dispute between them.]

He means: the assembly.

The interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing (in prayer) (64). And those who say: "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever-clinging (ghuram) (65). Indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode (66)﴾.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "And those who spend the night before their Lord" means they pray to God, alternating between prostration in their prayer and standing.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and standing﴾: it is the plural of *qa'im* (one standing), just as *siyam* is the plural of *sa'im* (one fasting). ﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, turn away from us the punishment of Hell"﴾ means: those who ask God to turn away from them His retribution and punishment, out of fear of it and dread.

* *

As for His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging (kana gharaman)﴾:

He means: the punishment of Hell is *gharaman*, a constant, persistent, inescapable clinging that never leaves those among the disbelievers who are punished by it, and destroys them. From the same root comes the saying "a man is *mughram*," meaning one burdened with debt (*al-ghurm* and *al-dayn*). From it is also called the creditor a *gharim*, because of his demand for his right and his insistence upon it from his debtor. From it is also said of a man who is infatuated with women: "He is *mughram* with women," and "so-and-so is *mughram* with so-and-so" when he cannot bear to be without him. From it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"If he punishes, his punishment will be *gharaman*, and if he gives generously, he will not care."

He means: if he punishes, his punishment will be a binding punishment that does not leave its object, destroying him.

And the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"And on the day of al-Nissar and the day of al-Jifar, there was punishment, and there was *gharam*."

[The verse is by Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, as the author says. In *al-Lisan* it is attributed to al-Tirimmah. It says: *al-gharam* is the binding punishment, lasting evil, affliction, love, passion, and what cannot be escaped. Al-Zajjaj said it is the most severe punishment in the language. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾. He also said: "And the day of al-Nissar..." And His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾ mean: constant, persistent, and binding. In al-Bakri's *Mu'jam maAsta'jam* (Cairo edition, p. 385), *al-Jifar* with a kasra on its first letter and the letter *ra* is a place in Najd, and it is the place Bishr ibn Abi Khazim meant in his words: "And the day of al-Jifar..." Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Jifar is in the lands of Banu Tamim. Al-Bakri said in the entry on al-Nissar: al-Nissar, with a kasra on its first letter, in the form of a plural, are small mountains likened to a vulture that has alighted. Abu Hatim mentioned this. He said elsewhere: they are three black rocky hills called *al-Ansur*. There Tayy, Asad and Ghatafan, who were allies of Banu 'Amir and Banu Tamim, attacked, and Tamim fled while Banu 'Amir held firm, and they killed them severely. Banu Tamim were angered on behalf of Banu 'Amir, gathered, and met them at the day of al-Jifar, where they suffered worse than Banu 'Amir had. Bishr ibn Abi Khazim said: "Tamim was angered that 'Amir was slain on the day of al-Nissar, so they were recompensed with al-Sayhalam."

I say: *al-Sayhalam* is the destroying calamity. In another narration: "fa-u'tibu" (they were given recompense).]

And it is said in the same sense: the punishment of Hell is ever-clinging for those who are in it.

With the like of what we have said concerning this, the people of *ta'wil* (interpretation) have said.

Mention of those who said so:

* Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Lani narrated to me, saying: al-Mu'afi ibn Imran al-Mawsili informed us, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: God questioned the disbelievers about His blessings, and they did not return them to Him, so He made them debtors (*aghramahum*), and He caused them to enter the Fire.

* He said: al-Mu'afi narrated to us from Abu al-Ash'hab, from al-Hasan, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: They knew that every creditor parts from his debtor, except the creditor of Hell.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾: *al-gharam* is evil.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding His words, ﴿indeed its punishment is ever-clinging﴾, he said: it does not part from him.

* *

As for His words, ﴿indeed it is evil as a place of settling and a place of abode﴾:

He says: indeed Hell is evil as a *mustaqarr* (place of settling) and *muqam* (place of abode). By *mustaqarr* He means the settled place (*al-qarar*), and by *muqam* the dwelling (*al-iqamah*). The meaning of the speech is as if to say: Hell is evil as a dwelling and a resting place. If the *mim* of *muqam* is vowelled with a *damma*, it is from *iqamah*; if it is vowelled with a *fatha*, it is from *qumtu* (I stood).
